rows.stem: An electron experiences a force \((1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-16}\ \mathrm{N})\ \hat{i}\) in an electric field \(\vec{\mathrm{E}}\). The electric field \(\vec{\mathrm{E}}\) is :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '1. (b)', with the option's value printed beside it and no working.

The keyed option is \(-\left(1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{3}\ \dfrac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}\right)\hat{i}\).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the force on a charge in an electric field is \(\vec{\mathrm{F}} = q\vec{\mathrm{E}}\), and for an electron \(q = -e = -1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}\). So

\(\vec{\mathrm{E}} = \dfrac{\vec{\mathrm{F}}}{q} = \dfrac{\left(1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-16}\ \mathrm{N}\right)\hat{i}}{-1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}} = -\left(1{\cdot}0\times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\right)\hat{i}\)

The magnitude comes from \(10^{-16}/10^{-19} = 10^{3}\), and the minus sign is the physics the question is testing: an electron is pushed OPPOSITE to the field it sits in, so a force along \(+\hat{i}\) can only come from a field along \(-\hat{i}\). The two choices carrying \(10^{-3}\) invert that ratio of exponents, multiplying by the electronic charge instead of dividing by it.

rows.stem: Which one of the following is **not** a scalar quantity ?
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '2. (a) Electric Field', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is 'Electric field'.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: electric field is defined as force per unit charge, \(\vec{\mathrm{E}} = \vec{\mathrm{F}}/q\). Force is a vector and charge is a scalar, so the field inherits a direction and is a vector quantity. Each of the other three is a scalar: voltage is work done per unit charge, resistivity is a single number characterising an isotropic material, and power is energy transferred per unit time. None of them has a direction associated with it. So the quantity that is not a scalar is the electric field.

rows.stem:
The current density due to drift of electrons in a conductor is given by :
(symbols have their usual meanings)
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '3. (d)', with the expression \(n e v_d\) printed beside it and no working.

The keyed option is \(n\,e\,v_d\).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: in a time \(\Delta t\) every electron within a distance \(v_d\,\Delta t\) of a chosen cross-section crosses it, so the charge that passes is \(\Delta q = n\left(\mathrm{A}\,v_d\,\Delta t\right)e\), where \(n\) is the number of free electrons per unit volume and \(\mathrm{A}\) the area of cross-section. The current is therefore \(\mathrm{I} = \Delta q/\Delta t = n e \mathrm{A} v_d\), and current density is current per unit area:

\(j = \dfrac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{A}} = n\,e\,v_d\)

The expression \(n e \mathrm{A} v_d\) is the CURRENT itself, not the current density; the remaining two divide by the electronic charge instead of multiplying by it, which cannot produce a current per unit area.

rows.subtopic: Ampere's Circuital Law and the Solenoid
rows.stem: Which of the following graphs correctly represents the variation of the magnitude of the magnetic field outside a straight infinite current carrying wire of radius ‘a’, as a function of distance ‘r’ from the centre of the wire ?

options.label: A
options.text: A straight line of negative slope, starting at a positive value of \(\mathrm{B}\) above \(r = a\) (marked by a dashed ordinate) and falling to meet the \(r\)-axis.

options.label: B
options.text: A straight line of negative slope, starting at a positive value of \(\mathrm{B}\) on the \(\mathrm{B}\)-axis at \(r = 0\) and falling to meet the \(r\)-axis.

options.label: C
options.text: A curve starting at a high value of \(\mathrm{B}\) above \(r = a\) (marked by a dashed ordinate), falling steeply and then flattening as \(r\) increases, without meeting the \(r\)-axis.

options.label: D
options.text: A curve starting at a high value of \(\mathrm{B}\) on the \(\mathrm{B}\)-axis at \(r = 0\), falling steeply and then flattening as \(r\) increases, without meeting the \(r\)-axis.

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — ALL FOUR OPTIONS ARE THE DRAWINGS: four \(\mathrm{B}\)-versus-\(r\) panels, each with both axes labelled (\(\mathrm{B}\) up, \(r\) across), an origin marked 0 and a tick marked 'a' on the \(r\)-axis, and no numbers anywhere. The option texts above are a neutral reading of the line each panel draws (linear vs hyperbolic decay; starting above \(r = a\) vs at \(r = 0\)) — the physics the question tests, that \(\mathrm{B} \propto 1/r\) for \(r > a\), is not stated. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '4. (c)', and it reproduces the keyed graph — a curve starting at a high value of \(\mathrm{B}\) above a dashed ordinate at \(r = a\), falling steeply and then flattening out without meeting the \(r\)-axis. No justification is printed.

The keyed option is the curve that starts at a high value of \(\mathrm{B}\) above \(r = a\), falls steeply and then flattens as \(r\) increases, without meeting the \(r\)-axis.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: apply Ampere's circuital law to a circle of radius \(r\) drawn concentric with the wire. By symmetry \(\mathrm{B}\) is constant along it and tangential, so

\(\oint\vec{\mathrm{B}}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mathrm{B}\,(2\pi r) = \mu_0\mathrm{I}\ \Rightarrow\ \mathrm{B} = \dfrac{\mu_0\mathrm{I}}{2\pi r}\quad (r > a)\)

Two features then decide which graph is right. First, \(\mathrm{B}\propto 1/r\) is a hyperbola, never a straight line, so the two straight-line graphs are ruled out. Second, the question asks only about the region OUTSIDE the wire, so the plot must begin at the surface \(r = a\) and not at \(r = 0\) — inside the wire the field instead rises linearly from zero, which is why the correct graph is blank to the left of the dashed ordinate. A \(1/r\) curve falls towards the \(r\)-axis asymptotically and never touches it.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: A particle of mass m and charge q moving with a uniform velocity \(\vec{v} = v_{0x}\,\hat{i} + v_{0y}\,\hat{j}\) enters a region with a magnetic field \(\vec{\mathrm{B}} = \mathrm{B}_0\,\hat{j}\). After some time, an electric field \(\vec{\mathrm{E}} = \mathrm{E}_0\,\hat{j}\) is also switched on in the region. The resulting path described by the particle will be :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '5. (d) a helix with increasing pitch.', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is 'a helix with increasing pitch'.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: with only the magnetic field present,

\(\vec{\mathrm{F}} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{\mathrm{B}} = q\left(v_{0x}\hat{i} + v_{0y}\hat{j}\right)\times \mathrm{B}_0\hat{j} = q\,v_{0x}\mathrm{B}_0\left(\hat{i}\times\hat{j}\right) = q\,v_{0x}\mathrm{B}_0\,\hat{k}\)

which has no component along \(\hat{j}\). So the velocity component PARALLEL to the field, \(v_{0y}\), is left untouched while the perpendicular component \(v_{0x}\) is bent into a circle in the \(x\)-\(z\) plane. Uniform translation along one axis combined with circular motion about it is a helix, and while only the magnetic field acts its pitch \(v_{0y}\mathrm{T}\) is constant.

Switching on \(\vec{\mathrm{E}} = \mathrm{E}_0\hat{j}\) adds a force \(q\mathrm{E}_0\hat{j}\) directed ALONG the helix axis, which steadily increases \(v_{0y}\). The period of the circular part, \(\mathrm{T} = 2\pi m/q\mathrm{B}_0\), does not depend on speed and so is unchanged, but the distance advanced in each turn keeps growing. The path is therefore a helix of increasing pitch.

rows.subtopic: AC Voltage Applied to an Inductor and a Capacitor
rows.stem: An inductor, a capacitor and a resistor are connected in series across an ac source of voltage. If the frequency of the source is decreased gradually, the reactance of :

options.label: A
options.text: both the inductor and the capacitor decreases.

options.label: B
options.text: inductor decreases and the capacitor increases.

options.label: C
options.text: both the inductor and the capacitor increases.

options.label: D
options.text: inductor increases and the capacitor decreases.

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '6. (b) inductor decreases and the capacitor increases', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is 'inductor decreases and the capacitor increases'.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the two reactances depend on frequency in opposite ways,

\(\mathrm{X_L} = \omega\mathrm{L} = 2\pi f\mathrm{L}\qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathrm{X_C} = \dfrac{1}{\omega\mathrm{C}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f\mathrm{C}}\)

Lowering \(f\) therefore lowers \(\mathrm{X_L}\) and raises \(\mathrm{X_C}\). Physically, an inductor opposes a CHANGE of current, so a slowly changing current is opposed less; a capacitor at low frequency has time to charge up almost fully each half cycle and so blocks the current, becoming an open circuit in the limit \(f\to 0\). The resistance \(\mathrm{R}\) is unaffected by frequency and plays no part here.

rows.stem: The electromagnetic radiations used to kill germs in water purifiers are called :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '7. (d) ultraviolet', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is 'Ultraviolet rays'.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: ultraviolet radiation has wavelengths of a few hundred nanometres, so each photon carries a few electronvolts — enough to break chemical bonds and to damage the DNA of bacteria and viruses, which stops them reproducing. That is exactly what a UV lamp in a water purifier is for. Infrared photons are an order of magnitude weaker and merely heat the water; X-rays and gamma rays would certainly kill the germs but are ionising radiation, hazardous to handle and shield, and quite unnecessary for the job.

rows.stem: In the wave picture of light, the intensity I of light is related to the amplitude A of the wave as :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '8. (c)', with the relation \(\mathrm{I}\propto \mathrm{A}^{2}\) printed beside it and no justification.

The keyed option is \(\mathrm{I} \propto \mathrm{A}^{2}\).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: intensity is the energy carried across unit area in unit time, and for any wave the energy density is proportional to the square of the amplitude. Doubling the amplitude of a light wave therefore makes it four times as intense.

This is the relation that lies behind the interference formula \(\mathrm{I} = \mathrm{I}_1 + \mathrm{I}_2 + 2\sqrt{\mathrm{I}_1\mathrm{I}_2}\cos\phi\): waves superpose by adding AMPLITUDES, and only after that addition is the result squared to get the intensity. If intensity were proportional to amplitude itself, no interference term could arise at all.

rows.stem: In a single-slit diffraction experiment, the width of the slit is halved. The width of the central maximum, in the diffraction pattern, will become :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '9. (b) twice', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is 'twice'.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the first minimum of a single slit of width \(a\) lies where \(a\sin\theta = \lambda\), so the angular half-width of the central maximum is \(\theta\approx\lambda/a\) and its linear width on a screen at distance \(\mathrm{D}\) is

\(\beta_0 = \dfrac{2\lambda\mathrm{D}}{a}\)

The width is inversely proportional to the slit width, so halving \(a\) doubles it. The idea worth carrying away is the one that sounds backwards on first hearing: a NARROWER slit spreads the light MORE.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: A graph is plotted between the stopping potential (on y-axis) and the frequency of incident radiation (on x-axis) for a metal. The product of the slope of the straight line obtained and the magnitude of charge on an electron is equal to :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '10. (a) h', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is \(h\).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: Einstein's photoelectric equation gives the stopping potential as \(e\mathrm{V}_0 = h\nu - \phi_0\), that is

\(\mathrm{V}_0 = \left(\dfrac{h}{e}\right)\nu - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\)

Plotted against frequency this is a straight line of slope \(h/e\) and intercept \(-\phi_0/e\). The slope is the same for every metal — only the intercept depends on the work function — so multiplying the slope by the magnitude of the electronic charge returns Planck's constant \(h\). That is precisely how Millikan measured \(h\) from photoelectric data.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: Light of frequency \(6{\cdot}4 \times 10^{14}\) Hz is incident on a metal of work function \(2{\cdot}14\) eV. The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons is about :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '11. (b) 0.51eV', and no working is printed.

The keyed option is \(0{\cdot}51\) eV.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme:

\(h\nu = 6{\cdot}63\times 10^{-34}\times 6{\cdot}4\times 10^{14} = 4{\cdot}24\times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\)

Dividing by \(1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19}\) converts this to \(2{\cdot}65\ \mathrm{eV}\). Einstein's photoelectric equation then gives

\(\mathrm{K_{max}} = h\nu - \phi_0 = 2{\cdot}65 - 2{\cdot}14 = 0{\cdot}51\ \mathrm{eV}\)

Note that converting the photon energy into electronvolts first is what keeps the arithmetic short — the work function is already quoted in electronvolts, so no second conversion is needed.

rows.subtopic: Line Spectra of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: The ratio of maximum frequency and minimum frequency of light emitted in Balmer series of hydrogen spectrum, in Bohr’s model is :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '12. (b)', with the fraction \(\dfrac{9}{5}\) printed beside it and no working.

The keyed option is \(\dfrac{9}{5}\).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: every line of the Balmer series ends on \(n = 2\), and in Bohr's model

\(h\nu = 13{\cdot}6\left(\dfrac{1}{2^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{n^{2}}\right)\ \mathrm{eV}\)

The MAXIMUM frequency is the largest such transition, the series limit \(n = \infty\to 2\), giving \(h\nu_{max} = \dfrac{13{\cdot}6}{4}\ \mathrm{eV}\). The MINIMUM frequency is the smallest transition that still belongs to the series, \(n = 3\to 2\), giving

\(h\nu_{min} = 13{\cdot}6\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{9}\right) = 13{\cdot}6\times\dfrac{5}{36}\ \mathrm{eV}\)

The ratio is therefore \(\dfrac{1/4}{5/36} = \dfrac{36}{20} = \dfrac{9}{5}\). The factor \(13{\cdot}6\) cancels between numerator and denominator, which is why the ratio comes out as a pure number, independent of any physical constant.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem: At a certain temperature in an intrinsic semiconductor, the electrons and holes concentration is \(1{\cdot}5 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\). When it is doped with a trivalent dopant, hole concentration increases to \(4{\cdot}5 \times 10^{22}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\). In the doped semiconductor, the concentration of electrons \((n_e)\) will be :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '13. (c)', with the value \(5\times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\) printed beside it and no working.

The keyed option is \(5 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: at a fixed temperature the law of mass action holds for a semiconductor whatever its doping,

\(n_e\,n_h = n_i^{2}\)

where \(n_i\) is the intrinsic carrier concentration. Here \(n_i = 1{\cdot}5\times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\), so \(n_i^{2} = 2{\cdot}25\times 10^{32}\ \mathrm{m^{-6}}\), and after doping

\(n_e = \dfrac{2{\cdot}25\times 10^{32}}{4{\cdot}5\times 10^{22}} = 5\times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\)

A trivalent dopant contributes acceptor levels, making the material p-type, so holes become the majority carriers and the electron concentration is pushed far BELOW its intrinsic value — from \(10^{16}\) down to \(10^{9}\). The value \(6{\cdot}75\times 10^{38}\) is what comes of multiplying the two given numbers instead of dividing.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: If a p-n junction diode is reverse biased,

options.label: D
options.text: the current is mainly due to majority carriers.

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '14. (c) the potential barrier is raised', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is 'the potential barrier is raised'.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: in reverse bias the battery's positive terminal is connected to the n-side and its negative terminal to the p-side, so the applied field inside the junction points the SAME way as the built-in field of the depletion region. The two add. The depletion layer widens, and the barrier height rises from \(\mathrm{V}_0\) to \(\mathrm{V}_0 + \mathrm{V}\).

Diffusion of majority carriers across the junction is then suppressed almost completely. The tiny current that still flows — the reverse saturation current, of the order of microamperes — is carried by MINORITY carriers swept across by the field, which is why the choice attributing the reverse current to majority carriers is also wrong.

rows.subtopic: AC Voltage Applied to a Resistor
rows.stem:
A voltage signal is described by :
\(v = \mathrm{V}_0\) for \(0 \le t \le \dfrac{\mathrm{T}}{2}\)
\(\quad\; = 0\) for \(\dfrac{\mathrm{T}}{2} \le t \le \mathrm{T}\)
for a cycle. Its rms value is :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '15. (a)', with \(\dfrac{\mathrm{V}_o}{\sqrt{2}}\) printed beside it and no working.

The keyed option is \(\dfrac{\mathrm{V}_0}{\sqrt{2}}\).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the rms value is the square root of the mean of \(v^{2}\) taken over one full cycle. Here \(v^{2} = \mathrm{V}_0^{2}\) for the first half of the period and \(0\) for the second, so

\(\overline{v^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{T}}\left(\mathrm{V}_0^{2}\cdot\dfrac{\mathrm{T}}{2} + 0\cdot\dfrac{\mathrm{T}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\mathrm{V}_0^{2}}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ v_{rms} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V}_0}{\sqrt{2}}\)

Worth noticing: this signal is not sinusoidal at all, yet the familiar factor \(1/\sqrt{2}\) still appears — and for a quite different reason. Here it comes from the signal being switched fully on for exactly half of each cycle, not from averaging \(\sin^{2}\omega t\).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The internal resistance of a cell is constant.
Reason (R) : Ionic concentration of the electrolyte remains same during use of a cell.
rows.context: Questions number 16 to 18 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '16. (d)', followed by that option restated — the Assertion false and the Reason false too — and no justification.

The keyed option is that the Assertion is false and the Reason is also false.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the internal resistance of a cell is not a fixed number. It depends on the separation and area of the electrodes, on the temperature, and — the point this question turns on — on the concentration of the electrolyte, since \(r\) varies as \(\dfrac{d}{\mathrm{A}\sigma}\) and the conductivity \(\sigma\) falls as the ions taking part in the electrode reactions are used up.

So as a cell is discharged its ionic concentration DOES change, the electrolyte conducts less well, and the internal resistance RISES. This is why a run-down cell can still show nearly its full emf on a high-resistance voltmeter and yet be unable to light a lamp: almost the whole emf is now dropped inside the cell itself.

The Assertion is therefore false, and the Reason is false as well. The two are worth separating even so, because it is the falsehood of the Reason that CAUSES the falsehood of the Assertion — the resistance changes precisely because the concentration does.

rows.subtopic: Torque on a Current Loop and Magnetic Dipole
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : When radius of a circular loop carrying a steady current is doubled, its magnetic moment becomes four times.
Reason (R) : The magnetic moment of a circular loop carrying a steady current is proportional to the area of the loop.
rows.context: Questions number 16 to 18 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '17. (a)', followed by that option restated — both statements true, with the Reason the correct explanation of the Assertion — and no justification.

The keyed option is that both statements are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the magnetic moment of a plane current loop is \(m = \mathrm{N}\mathrm{I}\mathrm{A}\), and for a single circular turn \(\mathrm{A} = \pi r^{2}\), so

\(m = \mathrm{I}\pi r^{2}\ \Rightarrow\ m\propto r^{2}\)

Doubling the radius quadruples the area and therefore quadruples the magnetic moment, provided the current is unchanged — which the question secures by saying 'steady current'. So the Assertion is true.

The Reason states the general proportionality \(m\propto\mathrm{A}\), which is true, and it is exactly the step that turns 'the radius doubled' into 'the moment became four times'. So both statements are true and the second genuinely explains the first.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The nucleus \({}^{7}_{3}\mathrm{X}\) is more stable than the nucleus \({}^{4}_{3}\mathrm{Y}\).
Reason (R) : \({}^{7}_{3}\mathrm{X}\) contains more number of protons.
rows.context: Questions number 16 to 18 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '18. (c)', followed by that option restated — the Assertion true but the Reason false — and no justification.

The keyed option is that the Assertion is true but the Reason is false.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the two nuclei named have the same atomic number \(\mathrm{Z} = 3\), so both are isotopes of lithium: \({}^{7}_{3}\mathrm{X}\) is lithium-7 and \({}^{4}_{3}\mathrm{Y}\) is lithium-4. Lithium-7 is the common, stable isotope, while lithium-4 lies far outside the band of stability — it has only one neutron for three protons and breaks up almost immediately by proton emission. So the Assertion is true.

The Reason, however, asserts something the symbols themselves contradict: the subscript is the proton number and it is \(3\) in BOTH nuclei, so they contain the SAME number of protons. What actually differs is the neutron number, four against one, and it is the extra neutrons — supplying attraction without adding Coulomb repulsion — that give the heavier isotope its much larger binding energy per nucleon and hence its stability. Adding protons alone would make a nucleus LESS stable, not more.

So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false.

rows.subtopic: Biot-Savart Law and Field of a Circular Loop
rows.stem: A wire of length \(l\) is in the form of a circular loop A of one turn. This loop is reshaped into loop B of three turns. Find the ratio of the magnetic fields at the centres of loop A and loop B for the same current through them.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

\(\mathrm{B} = \dfrac{\mu_0\mathrm{N}\mathrm{I}}{2r}\)

\(l = 2\pi r\ ;\qquad 2\pi r_A = 3\left(2\pi r_B\right)\)

\(r_B = \dfrac{r_A}{3}\)

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{B}_A}{\mathrm{B}_B} = \dfrac{\mu_0\mathrm{N}_A\mathrm{I}}{2r_A}\times\dfrac{2r_B}{\mu_0\mathrm{N}_B\mathrm{I}}\)

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{B}_A}{\mathrm{B}_B} = \dfrac{1}{9}\)

Marks: ½ for the field formula, ½ for the radius relation, ½ for setting up the ratio, ½ for the value.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the ratio reduces to \(\dfrac{\mathrm{B}_A}{\mathrm{B}_B} = \dfrac{\mathrm{N}_A}{\mathrm{N}_B}\cdot\dfrac{r_B}{r_A} = \dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{9}\). The two factors reinforce each other rather than cancelling: loop B has three times as many turns AND one third of the radius, and each of those alone would treble the field at the centre. Put generally, for a FIXED length of wire wound into \(\mathrm{N}\) turns, \(r\propto 1/\mathrm{N}\) and so \(\mathrm{B}\propto \mathrm{N}^{2}\) — which is why the field at the centre of the three-turn loop is nine times that of the one-turn loop carrying the same current.

rows.stem: What is meant by the term ‘displacement current’ ? Briefly explain how this current is different from a conduction current.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

Displacement current: it is the current that arises due to the rate of change of the electric field or flux.

Alternatively: \(\mathrm{I}_d = \varepsilon_0\left(\dfrac{d\phi_E}{dt}\right)\)

Alternatively: the term with the units of current, introduced to explain the continuity of current in a region.

Difference:
Displacement current is due to a change in electric flux.
Conduction current is due to the flow of electrons.

Alternatively, as formulas: \(\mathrm{I}_d = \varepsilon_0\left(\dfrac{d\phi_E}{dt}\right)\) and \(\mathrm{I}_c = \dfrac{dq}{dt}\).

Marks: 1 for the definition, 1 for the difference.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: Maxwell was driven to it because Ampere's circuital law gave two different answers for one loop. Take a circle round the wire feeding a charging capacitor. A flat surface spanning it is pierced by the wire and encloses the conduction current \(\mathrm{I}_c\); a bulging surface with the SAME boundary passes between the capacitor plates and encloses no current at all. The changing electric flux between the plates supplies exactly the missing term, and

\(\oint\vec{\mathrm{B}}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0\left(\mathrm{I}_c + \mathrm{I}_d\right)\)

now gives the same result for both surfaces. The deeper point is that displacement current needs no charge carriers whatever and exists in vacuum — which is what lets a changing electric field generate a magnetic field in empty space, and so allows electromagnetic waves to propagate at all.

rows.stem: State Huygens’ principle. How did Huygens explain the absence of the backwave ?
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

Statement: each point of the wavefront is the source of a secondary disturbance in all directions. The common tangent to all the secondary wavelets gives the new position of the wavefront.

Explanation of the absence of the backwave: light energy cannot travel in the backward direction.

Alternatively: it was an adhoc assumption.

Alternatively: for the back wave \(\mathrm{I} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 + \cos\theta\right)\); at \(\theta = 180^\circ\) the contribution is zero.

Alternatively: the amplitude of the secondary wavelets is maximum in the forward direction and zero in the backward direction.

Note: the scheme instructs that full credit be given for any other relevant explanation.

Marks: ½ + ½ for the statement, 1 for the explanation.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the obliquity factor \(\dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 + \cos\theta\right)\) is the modern repair of what Huygens himself simply assumed. It weights each secondary wavelet according to the angle \(\theta\) between the direction considered and the outward normal to the wavefront: at \(\theta = 0\) the factor is 1, so the forward wave has its full strength, and at \(\theta = 180^\circ\) it is 0, so the backward wave vanishes identically. Huygens could not justify this in his own time, which is why his construction is properly described as a geometrical recipe that works rather than a derivation.

rows.subtopic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves
rows.stem: Use Huygens’ principle to show reflection/refraction of a plane wave by (i) concave mirror, and (ii) a convex lens.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

The mark split is (i) diagram for the concave mirror, 1 mark, and (ii) diagram for the convex lens, 1 mark. The scheme prints the two ray diagrams and no prose, so they are described here.

(i) Concave mirror: a plane incident wavefront, drawn as a vertical line with arrows showing it travelling to the right, meets a concave mirror of radius \(\mathrm{R}\) whose reflecting surface faces the incoming wave. Each point of the arriving wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets. Because the edges of the mirror are reached before the centre of its concave face, the reflected wavelets are staggered, and their common tangent is a SPHERICAL wavefront of radius \(\mathrm{R}/2\) converging on the focus \(\mathrm{F}\).

(ii) Convex lens: a plane incident wavefront meets a convex lens. The lens is thickest at its centre, so the part of the wavefront passing through the middle spends the longest time in the slower medium and is retarded most, while the parts near the rim are held back least. The emerging wavefront is therefore spherical, of radius equal to the focal length \(f\), and converges to the focus.

Marks: 1 + 1.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the common thread is that Huygens' construction explains focusing purely as a DELAY — no ray has to be bent. The mirror makes the central path longer geometrically, because the centre of a concave surface is further from the incoming wavefront than the rim; the lens makes the central path longer OPTICALLY, because light there passes through more glass, in which it travels more slowly. In both cases the wavefront that emerges is spherical rather than plane, and a spherical wavefront converges on its own centre of curvature, which is the focus.

rows.stem: The refractive indices of two media A and B are 2 and \(\sqrt{2}\) respectively. What is the critical angle for their interface ?
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

From Snell's law:

\(\mu_A\sin i_c = \mu_B\sin 90^\circ\)

\(2\times\sin i_c = \sqrt{2}\times 1\)

\(\sin i_c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)

\(i_c = 45^\circ\)

Alternatively:

\(\sin i_c = \dfrac{1}{{}^{B}\mu_A}\ ,\qquad \sin i_c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ ,\qquad i_c = 45^\circ\)

Marks: ½ for each of the four steps on the first route, or 1 + ½ + ½ on the second.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: total internal reflection can only happen when light travels from the DENSER medium into the rarer one, so here the light must be passing from the medium of refractive index 2 into the medium of refractive index \(\sqrt{2}\), and the critical angle is measured in the denser medium. At the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the boundary, \(r = 90^\circ\), which is what puts \(\sin 90^\circ = 1\) on the right-hand side.

The two routes agree because the relative refractive index is \({}^{B}\mu_A = \dfrac{\mu_A}{\mu_B} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}\), so \(\sin i_c = 1/\sqrt{2}\) either way.

rows.stem: Draw a graph showing the variation of binding energy per nucleon as a function of mass number A. The binding energy per nucleon for heavy nuclei \((\mathrm{A} > 170)\) decreases with the increase in mass number. Explain.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

The scheme prints the standard binding-energy curve: binding energy per nucleon in MeV on the vertical axis against mass number \(\mathrm{A}\) on the horizontal, rising steeply from about 1 MeV at \({}^{2}\mathrm{H}\) through \({}^{4}\mathrm{He}\), \({}^{12}\mathrm{C}\) and \({}^{16}\mathrm{O}\), reaching a broad maximum of about \(8{\cdot}8\) MeV near \({}^{56}\mathrm{Fe}\), and then falling slowly to about \(7{\cdot}6\) MeV at \({}^{238}\mathrm{U}\).

Explanation: nuclear forces are short range and show saturation, while the electrostatic force is neither short range nor saturating. Hence for heavier nuclei \(\left(\mathrm{A} > 170\right)\) the electrostatic force of repulsion becomes predominant, decreasing the binding energy per nucleon.

Alternatively: as the size of the nucleus increases, the nucleus becomes unstable.

Note: the scheme deducts no marks if the values of the elements are not shown on the graph.

Marks: 1 for the graph, 1 for the explanation.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the contrast the scheme draws is essentially a counting argument. A nucleon is bound only by the few neighbours lying within the roughly \(2\ \mathrm{fm}\) range of the nuclear force — that is what saturation means — so the total attractive energy grows in proportion to \(\mathrm{A}\) and the energy PER nucleon levels off. The Coulomb repulsion has unlimited range, so every proton repels every other one and that energy grows like \(\mathrm{Z}\left(\mathrm{Z} - 1\right)\), faster than \(\mathrm{A}\). Beyond the iron region the second term is winning, and the curve turns over.

The same curve explains where nuclear energy comes from: moving TOWARDS the peak releases energy, so light nuclei release it by fusing and heavy nuclei by fissioning.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: Using Bohr’s postulates, obtain the expression for radius of \(n^{\text{th}}\) stable orbit in a hydrogen atom.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

\(\dfrac{m v^{2}}{r_n} = \dfrac{kq^{2}}{r_n^{2}} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_n^{2}}\) ..... (1)

\(m v r_n = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\) ..... (2)

Using equations (1) and (2):

\(r_n = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}\,4\pi\varepsilon_0}{m\left(2\pi\right)^{2}e^{2}} = 0{\cdot}53\times 10^{-10}\,n^{2}\ \mathrm{m}\)

Marks: ½ + ½ for the two postulates, 1 for the result.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the two starting equations ARE Bohr's postulates. The first says that the Coulomb attraction between the nucleus and the electron supplies exactly the centripetal force needed for a circular orbit; the second, the quantisation condition, says that only those orbits are allowed for which the angular momentum is an integer multiple of \(h/2\pi\).

The derivation is nothing more than eliminating \(v\) between them. From (2), \(v = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi m r_n}\); substituting into (1) and cancelling one power of \(r_n\) gives

\(r_n = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}\varepsilon_0}{\pi m e^{2}}\)

which is the scheme's expression written more compactly, since \(\dfrac{4\pi}{\left(2\pi\right)^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\). Putting the constants in gives \(r_1 = 0{\cdot}53\times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\), the Bohr radius; the \(n^{2}\) dependence means the allowed orbits spread out very rapidly, the fourth orbit already being sixteen times the size of the first.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: Explain the roles of diffusion current and drift current in the formation of the depletion layer in a p-n junction diode.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

During the formation of a p-n junction, and due to the concentration gradient across the p- and n-sides, holes diffuse from the p-side to the n-side \(\left(p\rightarrow n\right)\) and electrons diffuse from the n-side to the p-side \(\left(n\rightarrow p\right)\). When an electron diffuses from \(n\) to \(p\) it leaves behind an ionised donor — a positive charge — on the n-side, which is immobile. Similarly, when a hole diffuses from \(p\) to \(n\) due to the concentration gradient, it leaves behind an ionised acceptor — a negative charge — which is also immobile. This space-charge region on either side of the junction together is known as the depletion region.

As a result, an electric field is developed across the junction. Due to this field, an electron on the p-side of the junction moves to the n-side and a hole on the n-side of the junction moves to the p-side. The motion of charge carriers due to the electric field is called drift. Initially the diffusion current is large and the drift current is small.

As the diffusion process continues, the electric field strength and hence the drift current increases. This process continues till the diffusion and drift currents become equal.

Marks: 1 for the role of diffusion, 1 for the role of drift.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the two currents flow in OPPOSITE directions across the junction, which is what makes an equilibrium possible at all — diffusion carries majority carriers one way, drift carries minority carriers back the other. The equilibrium is dynamic rather than a stoppage: both currents go on flowing and their difference is zero, so the net current through an unbiased junction is zero.

The potential difference that has built up across the depletion region by then is the barrier potential \(\mathrm{V}_0\), typically about \(0{\cdot}3\ \mathrm{V}\) for germanium and \(0{\cdot}7\ \mathrm{V}\) for silicon. Note also that the depletion region is depleted of MOBILE carriers but not of charge — the ionised donors and acceptors are still there, fixed in the lattice, and they are the source of the field.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier
rows.stem: Explain the property of a p-n junction which makes it suitable for rectifying alternating voltages. Differentiate between a half-wave and a full-wave rectifier.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

A p-n junction conducts in forward bias.

Alternatively: a p-n junction is a uni-directional device.

The half-wave rectifier gives output only for half of the input cycle. The full-wave rectifier gives output for both halves of the input cycle.

Alternatively: if the output waveforms of both rectifiers are shown diagrammatically, full credit is to be given.

Marks: 1 for the property, 1 for the difference.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the property being exploited is extreme asymmetry. A forward-biased junction has a resistance of a few ohms, while a reverse-biased one has a resistance of the order of megohms, so during one half of the ac cycle current passes almost freely and during the other it is blocked almost completely. A device that passes current in only one direction turns an alternating input into a unidirectional output.

Beyond the scheme's one-line difference, the consequences are worth knowing. A half-wave rectifier uses a single diode and simply discards half of the input, so its output is a train of gaps and its ripple frequency equals the supply frequency. A full-wave rectifier uses two diodes with a centre-tapped transformer, or four in a bridge, so that BOTH half-cycles are routed through the load in the same direction; its output has twice the ripple frequency and about twice the average value, which makes it far easier to smooth with a filter capacitor.

rows.stem: A potential difference V is applied across a conductor of length \(l\) and uniform cross-section area A. How will the (i) electric field E, (ii) drift velocity \(v_d\), and (iii) current density j be affected when (a) V is doubled and (b) \(l\) is halved (keeping other factors constant) ?
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(a) When \(\mathrm{V}\) is doubled:
(i) the electric field is doubled;
(ii) the drift velocity is doubled;
(iii) the current density is doubled.

(b) When \(l\) is halved:
(i) the electric field is doubled;
(ii) the drift velocity is doubled;
(iii) the current density is doubled.

Alternatively, the scheme works each one from its formula:

(i) \(\mathrm{E} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V}}{l}\ ;\qquad \therefore\ \mathrm{E}' = 2\mathrm{E}\)

(ii) \(v_d = \left(\dfrac{e\mathrm{E}}{m}\right)\tau = \dfrac{e\tau}{m}\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{V}}{l}\right)\ ;\qquad \therefore\ v_d' = 2v_d\)

(iii) \(j = \dfrac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{A}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{RA}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{A}}\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{\rho l}\right) = \dfrac{\mathrm{V}}{\rho l}\ ;\qquad \therefore\ j\) is also doubled.

Marks: ½ for each of the six answers.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the reason all six answers come out the same is that each of the three quantities depends on the applied voltage and the length only through the RATIO \(\mathrm{V}/l\) — and doubling the numerator does exactly what halving the denominator does. Written out: \(\mathrm{E} = \mathrm{V}/l\), then \(v_d = \dfrac{e\tau}{m}\mathrm{E}\), then \(j = n e v_d\), so each follows from the one before by a constant factor. 'Keeping other factors constant' means the area of cross-section \(\mathrm{A}\), the carrier density \(n\) and the relaxation time \(\tau\) are all unchanged.

A note on the printed scheme rather than on the physics: in the 'Alternatively' block the second case is labelled (a) where the boxed mark split correctly calls it (b). Only the label slipped; the working under it is the \(l\)-halved case and is right.

rows.stem: What is meant by the term ‘mutual inductance’ of a pair of coils ? Obtain an expression for the mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids, each of length \(l\) but having different number of turns \(\mathrm{N}_1\) and \(\mathrm{N}_2\) and radii \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) \((r_2 > r_1)\).
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

Mutual inductance: it is the magnetic flux in the secondary coil due to the flow of unit current in the primary coil.

Alternatively: it is the emf induced in the secondary coil when the rate of change of current in the primary coil is unity.

Expression for mutual inductance: let \(\mathrm{N}_1\) and \(\mathrm{N}_2\) be the total number of turns of coils \(\mathrm{S}_1\) and \(\mathrm{S}_2\) respectively.

When a current \(\mathrm{I}_2\) is set up through \(\mathrm{S}_2\), it in turn sets up a magnetic flux through \(\mathrm{S}_1\):

\(\mathrm{N}_1\phi_1 = \mathrm{M}_{12}\mathrm{I}_2\) ..... (1)

where \(\mathrm{M}_{12}\) is the mutual inductance of solenoid \(\mathrm{S}_1\) with respect to \(\mathrm{S}_2\).

Magnetic field due to \(\mathrm{I}_2\) in \(\mathrm{S}_2\) is \(\mu_0\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{N}_2}{l}\right)\mathrm{I}_2\)

\(\mathrm{N}_1\phi_1 = \left(\mathrm{N}_1\right)\left(\pi r_1^{2}\right)\left(\mu_0\dfrac{\mathrm{N}_2}{l}\mathrm{I}_2\right)\) ..... (2)

From equations (1) and (2):

\(\mathrm{M}_{12} = \dfrac{\mu_0\mathrm{N}_1\mathrm{N}_2\pi r_1^{2}}{l}\)

Marks: 1 for the meaning, 2 for the derivation (½ for each of its four steps).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: two details carry the result. First, the area that appears is \(\pi r_1^{2}\), the cross-section of the INNER solenoid, not \(\pi r_2^{2}\). The field of the outer solenoid is uniform throughout its interior, so the flux actually linked with the inner coil is set by the inner coil's own area — the outer solenoid's extra cross-section links no turns of \(\mathrm{S}_1\).

Second, the answer is symmetric. Repeating the argument the other way round, with the current in \(\mathrm{S}_1\) and the flux computed through \(\mathrm{S}_2\), gives the same expression, so \(\mathrm{M}_{12} = \mathrm{M}_{21} = \mathrm{M}\) and one can speak simply of 'the mutual inductance of the pair'. Writing \(n_1 = \mathrm{N}_1/l\) and \(n_2 = \mathrm{N}_2/l\) for the turns per unit length puts it in its more familiar form, \(\mathrm{M} = \mu_0 n_1 n_2\pi r_1^{2}\,l\).

rows.subtopic: AC Voltage Applied to an Inductor and a Capacitor
rows.stem: An ac source \(v = v_m \sin \omega t\) is connected across an ideal capacitor. Derive the expression for the (i) current flowing in the circuit, and (ii) reactance of the capacitor. Plot a graph of current i versus \(\omega t\).
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) \(\mathrm{V}_m\sin\omega t = \dfrac{q}{\mathrm{C}}\)

\(\mathrm{I} = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\mathrm{C}\mathrm{V}_m\sin\omega t\right)\)

\(\mathrm{I} = \omega\mathrm{C}\mathrm{V}_m\cos\omega t\)

Alternatively: \(\mathrm{I} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V}_m}{1/\omega\mathrm{C}}\cos\omega t = \mathrm{I}_m\sin\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\)

(ii) \(\mathrm{I} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V}_m}{1/\omega\mathrm{C}}\sin\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \mathrm{I}_m\sin\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\)

Comparing with \(\mathrm{I}_m = \dfrac{\mathrm{V}_m}{1/\omega\mathrm{C}}\), the reactance of the capacitor is

\(\mathrm{X}_c = \dfrac{1}{\omega\mathrm{C}}\)

The scheme also prints the required graph: voltage and current plotted together against \(\omega t\) on the same axes over rather more than one full cycle, the voltage as a solid curve and the current as a dashed one, with a chosen instant \(\omega t_1\) marked by dashed construction lines to the two instantaneous values. The current curve runs a quarter of a cycle AHEAD of the voltage curve — it starts at its maximum at \(\omega t = 0\), where the voltage is zero and rising, and it is zero at \(\omega t = \pi/2\), where the voltage peaks.

Marks: 1 for the current, 1 for the reactance, 1 for the graph.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: for an ideal capacitor connected straight across the source there is no resistive drop, so the loop rule gives \(v = q/\mathrm{C}\) at every instant. The CHARGE is therefore in phase with the applied voltage, and the current, being its time derivative, is a quarter of a cycle ahead of it — which is the content of the phase \(+\pi/2\) in the answer and of the graph.

Comparing \(\mathrm{I}_m = \dfrac{\mathrm{V}_m}{1/\omega\mathrm{C}}\) with Ohm's law identifies \(1/\omega\mathrm{C}\) as the quantity playing the part of resistance; it is called reactance rather than resistance because it dissipates nothing. The average power is \(\mathrm{V}_{rms}\mathrm{I}_{rms}\cos\phi\) with \(\phi = \pi/2\), so \(\cos\phi = 0\): energy is stored in the field during one quarter cycle and returned to the source in the next.

rows.subtopic: Power in AC Circuits and the Power Factor
rows.stem: A series combination of an inductor L, a capacitor C and a resistor R is connected across an ac source of voltage in a circuit. Obtain an expression for the average power consumed by the circuit. Find power factor for (i) purely inductive circuit, and (ii) purely resistive circuit.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

Instantaneous power:

\(\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{V}\mathrm{I} = \left(\mathrm{V}_m\sin\omega t\right)\times \mathrm{I}_m\sin\left(\omega t + \phi\right)\)

\(\mathrm{P} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V}_m\mathrm{I}_m}{2}\left[\cos\phi - \cos\left(2\omega t + \phi\right)\right]\) ..... (1)

The average power over a cycle is given by the average of the two terms on the right-hand side of equation (1). It is only the second term which is time dependent; its average is zero, because the positive half of the cosine cancels the negative half. Therefore

\(\mathrm{P}_{avg} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V}_m\mathrm{I}_m}{2}\cos\phi = \dfrac{\mathrm{V}_m}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\dfrac{\mathrm{I}_m}{\sqrt{2}}\cos\phi\)

\(\mathrm{P}_{avg} = \mathrm{V}_{rms}\mathrm{I}_{rms}\cos\phi\)

Alternatively: if the expression is deduced using integration, full credit is to be given.

(i) Power factor for a purely inductive circuit: \(\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ \cos\phi = 0\).

(ii) Power factor for a purely resistive circuit: \(\phi = 0\ \Rightarrow\ \cos\phi = 1\).

Marks: 2 for the expression, ½ + ½ for the two power factors.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the step from the product to the bracket is the identity \(\sin\mathrm{X}\sin\mathrm{Y} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\cos\left(\mathrm{X}-\mathrm{Y}\right) - \cos\left(\mathrm{X}+\mathrm{Y}\right)\right]\), which turns the product of two sinusoids into a CONSTANT term plus an oscillation at twice the source frequency. Only the constant survives averaging, and it carries the whole of the average power.

The two special cases repay reading physically rather than as substitutions. A pure inductor or capacitor gives back to the source, in one quarter cycle, exactly the energy it absorbed in the previous one, so its average power consumption is zero no matter how large the current — this is the 'wattless current'. A pure resistor has voltage and current in step, so the product is positive at every instant and energy is dissipated continuously, giving a power factor of 1.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.stem: Calculate the wavelength of de Broglie waves associated with a proton having \(\left(\dfrac{500}{1{\cdot}673}\right)\) eV energy. How will the wavelength be affected for an alpha particle having the same energy ?
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m\mathrm{K}}}\)

\(\mathrm{K} = \left(\dfrac{500}{1{\cdot}673}\right)\mathrm{eV} = \dfrac{500\times 1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19}}{1{\cdot}673}\ \mathrm{J}\)

\(\lambda_p = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63\times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2\times 1{\cdot}673\times 10^{-27}\times\left(\dfrac{500\times 1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19}}{1{\cdot}673}\right)}} = 1{\cdot}65\times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}\)

\(\lambda\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\)

For an \(\alpha\) particle, \(m_\alpha = 4m_p\), and therefore

\(\lambda_\alpha = \dfrac{\lambda_p}{2}\)

Marks: ½ for the formula, ½ for the energy in joules, ½ for the substitution, ½ for the value, ½ for the mass dependence, ½ for the result.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the awkward-looking energy \(\left(500/1{\cdot}673\right)\mathrm{eV}\) is chosen precisely so that the \(1{\cdot}673\) cancels the proton mass. Under the root,

\(2\times\left(1{\cdot}673\times 10^{-27}\right)\times\dfrac{500\times 1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19}}{1{\cdot}673} = 2\times 10^{-27}\times 500\times 1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19} = 1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-43}\)

whose square root is exactly \(4{\cdot}0\times 10^{-22}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\), leaving \(\lambda = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63\times 10^{-34}}{4{\cdot}0\times 10^{-22}}\), the printed \(1{\cdot}65\times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}\).

For the second part, note that \(\lambda = h/\sqrt{2m\mathrm{K}}\) contains the mass and the kinetic energy but NOT the charge, so the alpha particle's doubled charge plays no part whatever. Its wavelength is halved purely because its mass is four times that of the proton, and \(\sqrt{4} = 2\).

rows.stem:
(i) Prove that the nuclear density is same for all nuclei.
(ii) Draw a plot of potential energy of a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation. Draw two inferences from this plot.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) \(\rho = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} = \dfrac{\text{mass number}\times\text{mass of nucleon}}{\text{volume of nucleus}}\)

\(\rho = \dfrac{\mathrm{A}\times m}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi\left(\mathrm{R}_0\mathrm{A}^{1/3}\right)^{3}} = \dfrac{3m}{4\pi\mathrm{R}_0^{3}}\)

Hence the density is independent of the mass number.

(ii) The scheme prints the nucleon-nucleon potential-energy curve: potential energy on the vertical axis against separation \(r\) on the horizontal, very large and positive at small \(r\), crossing zero, dipping to a minimum at \(r = r_0\), and then rising back towards zero as \(r\) increases. The region \(r < r_0\) is marked 'repulsion' and the region \(r > r_0\) is marked 'attraction'.

Inferences:
- The force is attractive for distances larger than \(r_0\).
- The force is repulsive for distances less than \(r_0\).

Alternatively: any other relevant inference drawn from the graph should be given full credit.

Marks: ½ + ½ for the proof, 1 for the graph, ½ + ½ for the two inferences.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the cancellation is the whole content of part (i). The empirical nuclear radius is \(\mathrm{R} = \mathrm{R}_0\mathrm{A}^{1/3}\), so the VOLUME is proportional to \(\mathrm{A}\); the mass is also proportional to \(\mathrm{A}\); and dividing one by the other leaves a constant in which \(\mathrm{A}\) does not appear at all. Numerically, with \(\mathrm{R}_0 = 1{\cdot}2\times 10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}\) and \(m = 1{\cdot}67\times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}\), the value is about \(2{\cdot}3\times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\) for every nucleus — some \(10^{14}\) times the density of water.

For part (ii) the inferences follow from the SLOPE, because the force is \(\mathrm{F} = -\dfrac{d\mathrm{U}}{dr}\). Beyond \(r_0\) the curve rises as \(r\) increases, so the slope is positive and the force is directed inwards, that is attractive. Inside \(r_0\) the curve falls very steeply as \(r\) increases, so the force is outwards and strongly repulsive — this hard core is what stops nucleons from collapsing into one another and gives a nucleus a roughly fixed density.

rows.stem:
(i) Draw a graph to show the variation of the number of scattered particles detected (N) in Geiger-Marsden experiment as a function of scattering angle \((\theta)\).
(ii) Discuss briefly two conclusions that can be drawn from this graph and how they lead to the discovery of nucleus in an atom.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) The scheme prints the Geiger-Marsden result: the number of scattered particles detected on the vertical axis, drawn on a logarithmic scale from \(10\) to \(10^{7}\), against the scattering angle \(\theta\) in degrees from \(0\) to \(180\) on the horizontal. The curve begins just below \(10^{7}\) at small angles, falls extremely steeply — it is already down to about \(10^{3}\) by \(50^\circ\) — and then flattens out a little below \(10^{2}\) beyond about \(120^\circ\), staying almost level all the way to \(180^\circ\).

(ii) Conclusions:
- The entire positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in a small space.
- Many of the \(\alpha\)-particles pass through the foil, which means that they do not suffer any collisions.

To deflect an \(\alpha\)-particle backwards, a large repulsive force is required, which is provided only if the greater part of the mass of the atom and its positive charge were concentrated tightly at its centre. This led to the discovery of the nucleus in the atom.

Marks: 1 for the graph, ½ + ½ for the two conclusions, 1 for the link to the discovery of the nucleus.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the force of the argument lies in the NUMBERS on that vertical axis, which is why it has to be drawn on a logarithmic scale — the count falls by five or six powers of ten across the plot. Roughly one \(\alpha\)-particle in eight thousand was turned through more than \(90^\circ\): rare enough to show that almost all of the atom is empty space, yet far too frequent to be an accident.

A Thomson 'plum pudding' atom, with its positive charge spread uniformly through the whole atomic volume, can only produce small deflections that build up gradually, and it cannot give a single large-angle scattering at all. Rutherford's own remark was that it was about as credible as firing a 15-inch shell at a sheet of tissue paper and having it come back and hit you.

rows.stem:
(i) Define electric flux and write its SI unit.
(ii) Use Gauss’ law to obtain the expression for the electric field due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet.
(iii) A cube of side L is kept in space, as shown in the figure. An electric field \(\vec{\mathrm{E}} = (\mathrm{A}x + \mathrm{B})\ \hat{i}\ \dfrac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}\) exists in the region. Find the net charge enclosed by the cube.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem of part (iii) says only ‘as shown in the figure’, so the cube's POSITION relative to the axes is the question. Described: right-handed x, y, z axes are drawn (y up, x to the right, z toward the lower left) with a cube drawn in outline, hidden edges dashed, and a vertical dimension arrow to the right of it labelled L. Withheld: which vertex of the cube sits on the origin and which pair of faces is perpendicular to x — that is exactly what fixes the flux and therefore the answer. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) \(\phi = \vec{\mathrm{E}}\cdot\vec{\mathrm{A}}\)

Alternatively: electric flux is the number of electric field lines passing through an area normally.

SI unit of electric flux: \(\mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-1}}\), or \(\mathrm{V\,m}\).

(ii) The scheme prints the Gaussian surface: a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet of surface charge density \(\sigma\), with a cylindrical pillbox pushed through it symmetrically so that its two flat end faces, each of area \(\mathrm{A}\), lie parallel to the sheet at equal distances on either side, and \(\vec{\mathrm{E}}\) points outwards along the axis, normal to both faces.

From Gauss's law:

\(\phi = \oint\vec{\mathrm{E}}\cdot d\vec{\mathrm{A}} = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\)

\(2\mathrm{E}\mathrm{A} = \dfrac{\sigma\mathrm{A}}{\varepsilon_0}\)

\(\mathrm{E} = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\)

Alternatively: if the shape of the Gaussian surface is taken cylindrical, full credit is to be given.

(iii) \(\phi_L = \mathrm{E}\,ds\cos 180^\circ = -\mathrm{E}\,ds = -\mathrm{B}\mathrm{L}^{2}\)

\(\phi_R = \mathrm{E}\,ds\cos 0^\circ = \mathrm{E}\,ds = \left(\mathrm{A}\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{B}\right)\mathrm{L}^{2} = \mathrm{A}\mathrm{L}^{3} + \mathrm{B}\mathrm{L}^{2}\)

Net flux \(= \phi_L + \phi_R = \left(\mathrm{A}\mathrm{L}^{3} + \mathrm{B}\mathrm{L}^{2}\right) - \mathrm{B}\mathrm{L}^{2}\)

Net flux \(= \mathrm{A}\mathrm{L}^{3} = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\ \Rightarrow\ q = \mathrm{A}\mathrm{L}^{3}\varepsilon_0\)

Marks: ½ + ½ for the definition and the unit, 2 for the plane-sheet derivation, 2 for the enclosed charge.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the figure fixes the geometry the scheme's part (iii) assumes. The cube sits with one vertex at the origin and its edges along the axes, so its left face lies in the \(y\)-\(z\) plane at \(x = 0\) and its right face at \(x = \mathrm{L}\); each face has area \(\mathrm{L}^{2}\).

Because \(\vec{\mathrm{E}}\) points along \(\hat{i}\), the four faces that contain the \(x\)-direction have the field lying IN them — the field is perpendicular to their outward normals — so they contribute no flux at all, and only the two faces perpendicular to \(x\) matter. On the left face the field is \(\mathrm{E} = \mathrm{A}\left(0\right) + \mathrm{B} = \mathrm{B}\) while the outward normal points along \(-\hat{i}\), which is where the \(\cos 180^\circ\) comes from; on the right face \(\mathrm{E} = \mathrm{A}\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{B}\) with the outward normal along \(+\hat{i}\).

The uniform part \(\mathrm{B}\) therefore cancels between the two faces — a uniform field encloses no net charge, whatever surface you draw — and only the part of the field that VARIES across the cube survives, giving \(q = \varepsilon_0\mathrm{A}\mathrm{L}^{3}\). Note that \(\mathrm{A}\) here has units \(\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}\,m^{-1}}\), so \(\varepsilon_0\mathrm{A}\mathrm{L}^{3}\) does come out in coulombs.

One point in part (ii) is worth pausing on: the factor 2 in \(2\mathrm{E}\mathrm{A}\) arises because the pillbox has TWO end faces and the field emerges through both. That is exactly why the answer is \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\) and not \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\) — the latter is the field just outside a charged CONDUCTOR, where the charge resides on a single surface and the field on the inner side is zero.

rows.stem:
(i) Define electric potential at a point and write its SI unit.
(ii) Two capacitors are connected in series. Derive an expression of the equivalent capacitance of the combination.
(iii) Two point charges + q and – q are located at points (3a, 0) and (0, 4a) respectively in x-y plane. A third charge Q is kept at the origin. Find the value of Q, in terms of q and a, so that the electrostatic potential energy of the system is zero.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) Electrostatic potential at any point in a region with an electrostatic field is the work done in bringing a unit positive charge, without acceleration, from infinity to that point.

Alternatively: \(\mathrm{V} = \dfrac{\text{Work Done}}{q}\), or \(\mathrm{V} = -\int\vec{\mathrm{E}}\cdot d\vec{l}\).

The SI unit of electrostatic potential is the volt. Alternatively, \(\mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}\).

(ii) The scheme prints two capacitors \(\mathrm{C}_1\) and \(\mathrm{C}_2\) in series across a supply, the facing plates carrying \(+\mathrm{Q}\) and \(-\mathrm{Q}\) so that the same charge \(\mathrm{Q}\) appears on every plate.

\(\mathrm{V} = \mathrm{V}_1 + \mathrm{V}_2 = \dfrac{\mathrm{Q}}{\mathrm{C}_1} + \dfrac{\mathrm{Q}}{\mathrm{C}_2}\)

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{Q}}{\mathrm{C}_{eq}} = \mathrm{Q}\left(\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{C}_1} + \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{C}_2}\right)\)

\(\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{C}_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{C}_1} + \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{C}_2}\)

(iii) Potential energy of the system \(= k\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{Q}\left(-q\right)}{4a} + \dfrac{\mathrm{Q}q}{3a} - \dfrac{q^{2}}{5a}\right]\)

Setting the potential energy of the system to zero:

\(\Rightarrow k\left[\dfrac{-\mathrm{Q}q}{4a} + \dfrac{\mathrm{Q}q}{3a} - \dfrac{q^{2}}{5a}\right] = 0\)

\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{-\mathrm{Q}}{4} + \dfrac{\mathrm{Q}}{3} - \dfrac{q}{5} = 0\)

\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{\mathrm{Q}}{12} - \dfrac{q}{5} = 0\)

\(\Rightarrow \mathrm{Q} = +\dfrac{12q}{5}\)

Marks: ½ + ½ for the definition and the unit, 2 for the equivalent capacitance, 2 for the value of the third charge.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the three separations in part (iii) come straight from the coordinates. The charge \(+q\) at \(\left(3a, 0\right)\) is a distance \(3a\) from the origin; the charge \(-q\) at \(\left(0, 4a\right)\) is \(4a\) from it; and the two of them are

\(\sqrt{\left(3a\right)^{2} + \left(4a\right)^{2}} = 5a\)

apart — a 3-4-5 right triangle, which is why the arithmetic closes so neatly. The potential energy of a system of three charges is the sum over the three PAIRS, each counted once, and each pair contributes \(k\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r_{12}}\).

The term \(-\dfrac{q^{2}}{5a}\) does not contain the unknown, so it is a fixed negative amount which the other two terms must cancel. Since \(\dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{12}\) is positive, the unknown charge must be positive, and \(\dfrac{\mathrm{Q}}{12} = \dfrac{q}{5}\) gives \(\mathrm{Q} = \dfrac{12q}{5} = 2{\cdot}4\,q\). The answer is independent of \(a\), because every separation scales with \(a\) and so the common factor \(1/a\) divides out.

In part (ii) the step that makes the derivation work is that a series combination forces the SAME charge onto each capacitor — the plates between them are isolated, so whatever charge leaves one must appear on the next — while the voltages add. That is the exact opposite of the parallel case, where the voltage is common and the charges add.

rows.stem:
(i) Write the principle and explain the working of a moving coil galvanometer. A galvanometer as such cannot be used to measure the current in a circuit. Why ?
(ii) Why is the magnetic field made radial in a moving coil galvanometer ? How is it achieved ?
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) Principle: when a rectangular loop carrying current \(\mathrm{I}\) is placed in a uniform magnetic field, it experiences a torque.

Working: when a current flows through the coil of a galvanometer, a torque acts on it,

\(\tau = \mathrm{N}i\mathrm{A}\mathrm{B}\sin\theta\)

For a radial magnetic field, \(\sin\theta = 1\). The spring provides a counter or restoring torque \(k\phi\), so

\(k\phi = \mathrm{N}i\mathrm{A}\mathrm{B}\)

and in equilibrium

\(\phi = \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{N}\mathrm{A}\mathrm{B}}{k}\right)i\)

A galvanometer cannot be used as such to measure current because it has a large resistance and hence will change the value of the current in the circuit; and because it is a sensitive device. (Any one of these is accepted.)

(ii) The magnetic field is made radial in a moving coil galvanometer so that the magnetic dipole moment \(\left(\vec{m}\right)\) is always perpendicular to the magnetic field \(\left(\vec{\mathrm{B}}\right)\), hence \(\sin\theta = 1\) always.

Alternatively: the magnetic field is made radial to make the scale linear.

It is achieved by using curved magnetic poles. Alternatively, by using a soft iron cylindrical core.

Marks: 1 for the principle, 1 for the working, 1 for why it cannot be used as such, 1 for the reason the field is radial, 1 for how the radial field is achieved.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the two objections in part (i) are worth separating. 'Sensitive' means the coil deflects through the whole scale for a current of the order of microamperes, so any ordinary circuit current would drive the pointer far past the end of the scale. 'Large resistance' is the more serious fault in principle: an ammeter must be connected in SERIES, so inserting a high-resistance instrument would reduce the very current it was brought in to measure. Both are cured at once by connecting a small resistance, the shunt, in parallel with the coil.

The linearity point behind part (ii) deserves stating explicitly. In a uniform field the deflection would satisfy \(k\phi = \mathrm{N}i\mathrm{A}\mathrm{B}\sin\theta\) with \(\theta\) itself changing as the coil turns, so \(\phi\) would not be proportional to \(i\) and equal current steps would give unequal deflections — the scale could not be divided evenly. In a radial field the plane of the coil always contains the field direction, so the normal to the coil, and with it \(\vec{m}\), stays perpendicular to \(\vec{\mathrm{B}}\) whatever the deflection; \(\sin\theta\) is permanently 1 and \(\phi\propto i\) exactly. The soft iron core has a second benefit: it concentrates the flux and so increases the sensitivity as well as shaping the field.

rows.subtopic: Biot-Savart Law and Field of a Circular Loop
rows.stem:
(i) Derive an expression for magnetic field on the axis of a current carrying circular loop.
(ii) Write any two points of difference between a diamagnetic and a paramagnetic substance.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) The scheme prints the standard diagram: a circular loop of radius \(\mathrm{R}\) carrying current \(i\), centred at \(\mathrm{O}\) with its plane perpendicular to the \(x\)-axis, and the field point \(\mathrm{P}\) on the axis at a distance \(x\) from the centre; a current element \(d\vec{l}\) at the top of the loop, the vector \(\vec{r}\) from it to \(\mathrm{P}\), and the resulting \(d\vec{\mathrm{B}}\) resolved into an axial component \(d\mathrm{B}_x\) and a perpendicular component \(d\mathrm{B}_\perp\), with the angle \(\theta\) between \(d\vec{\mathrm{B}}\) and the axis marked at \(\mathrm{P}\).

\(d\mathrm{B} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{i\left|d\vec{l}\times\vec{r}\right|}{r^{3}} = \dfrac{\mu_0\,i\,dl\,\sin 90^\circ}{4\pi\left(x^{2} + \mathrm{R}^{2}\right)}\)

\(d\mathrm{B}_\perp\) cancels out.

Net \(\mathrm{B} = \displaystyle\int d\mathrm{B}_x = \int d\mathrm{B}\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\dfrac{i\,dl}{\left(x^{2} + \mathrm{R}^{2}\right)}\times\dfrac{\mathrm{R}}{\left(x^{2} + \mathrm{R}^{2}\right)^{1/2}}\)

\(= \dfrac{\mu_0 i\mathrm{R}}{4\pi\left(x^{2} + \mathrm{R}^{2}\right)^{3/2}}\displaystyle\int dl = \dfrac{\mu_0 i\mathrm{R}}{4\pi\left(x^{2} + \mathrm{R}^{2}\right)^{3/2}}\left(2\pi\mathrm{R}\right)\)

\(\vec{\mathrm{B}} = \mathrm{B}_x\hat{i} = \dfrac{\mu_0\,i\,\mathrm{R}^{2}}{2\left(x^{2} + \mathrm{R}^{2}\right)^{3/2}}\,\hat{i}\)

(ii) Differences — any two of the following:

| Diamagnetic materials | Paramagnetic materials |
|---|---|
| Susceptibility lies between \(-1\) and \(0\). | Susceptibility is a small positive number, slightly greater than zero. |
| Relative permeability lies between \(0\) and \(1\). | Relative permeability is slightly greater than 1. |
| \(\mu < \mu_0\) | \(\mu > \mu_0\) |
| Tends to move from the stronger to the weaker part of an external field. | Tends to move from a region of weak field to one of strong field. |
| Is repelled by a magnet. | Is weakly attracted by a magnet. |
| The field inside the material is reduced, and field lines are expelled from it. | The field inside is slightly enhanced, and field lines are drawn into it. |

Marks: 3 for the derivation, 1 + 1 for the two differences.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: two steps carry the physics of the derivation. First, for a point on the AXIS the current element \(d\vec{l}\) is always perpendicular to \(\vec{r}\), which is why \(\sin 90^\circ = 1\) and the Biot-Savart magnitude comes out so simply; and \(r^{2} = x^{2} + \mathrm{R}^{2}\) by Pythagoras, the same for every element round the loop.

Second, the cancellation is a symmetry argument, not an approximation: the element diametrically OPPOSITE any given one contributes a \(d\mathrm{B}_\perp\) equal in size and opposite in direction, so summing right round the loop leaves only the axial components.

The projection factor is worth a second look, because it is \(\mathrm{R}\) and not \(x\) that appears on top:

\(\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathrm{R}}{\sqrt{x^{2} + \mathrm{R}^{2}}}\)

This is because \(d\vec{\mathrm{B}}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{r}\), so the angle \(d\vec{\mathrm{B}}\) makes with the axis is the COMPLEMENT of the angle \(\vec{r}\) makes with it. As a check, putting \(x = 0\) recovers the familiar field at the centre of a loop, \(\mathrm{B} = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{2\mathrm{R}}\), and for \(x \gg \mathrm{R}\) it becomes \(\mathrm{B}\approx\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{x^{3}}\) with \(m = i\pi\mathrm{R}^{2}\) — the axial field of a magnetic dipole.

rows.stem:
(i) Draw a ray diagram showing the formation of a real image of an object placed at a distance ‘u’ in front of a concave mirror of radius of curvature ‘R’. Hence, obtain the relation for the image distance ‘v’ in terms of u and R.
(ii) A \(1{\cdot}8\) m tall person stands in front of a convex lens of focal length 1 m, at a distance of 5 m. Find the position and height of the image formed.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) The scheme prints the ray diagram: an object \(\mathrm{AB}\) standing on the principal axis beyond the centre of curvature of a concave mirror with pole \(\mathrm{P}\), focus \(\mathrm{F}\) and centre of curvature \(\mathrm{C}\). A ray \(\mathrm{AM}\) parallel to the axis is reflected through \(\mathrm{F}\), and a second ray through \(\mathrm{F}\) is reflected parallel to the axis; the two meet at \(\mathrm{A}'\), forming the real, inverted image \(\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{B}'\) between \(\mathrm{C}\) and \(\mathrm{F}\). The distances \(u\), \(v\) and \(f\) are marked from the pole.

From the figure the two right-angled triangles \(\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{F}\) and \(\mathrm{MPF}\) are similar. (For paraxial rays, \(\mathrm{MP}\) can be considered to be a straight line perpendicular to \(\mathrm{CP}\).) Therefore

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{A}'}{\mathrm{PM}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{FP}}\ ,\qquad\text{or}\qquad \dfrac{\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{A}'}{\mathrm{BA}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{FP}}\quad\left(\because\ \mathrm{PM} = \mathrm{AB}\right)\) ..... (i)

Since \(\angle\mathrm{APB} = \angle\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{PB}'\), the right-angled triangles \(\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{P}\) and \(\mathrm{ABP}\) are also similar. Therefore

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{A}'}{\mathrm{BA}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{BP}}\) ..... (ii)

Comparing equations (i) and (ii):

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{FP}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{P} - \mathrm{FP}}{\mathrm{FP}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{BP}}\) ..... (iii)

With the sign convention \(\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{P} = -v\), \(\mathrm{FP} = -f\), \(\mathrm{BP} = -u\), equation (iii) gives

\(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{2}{\mathrm{R}}\)

Alternatively: if the result is derived by any other method, full credit is to be given.

(ii) For the lens, \(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\), with \(u = -5\ \mathrm{m}\) and \(f = +1\ \mathrm{m}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{-5} = \dfrac{1}{+1}\ \Rightarrow\ v = \dfrac{5}{4}\ \mathrm{m} = 1{\cdot}25\ \mathrm{m}\)

\(m = \dfrac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{O}} = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{+5/4}{-5} = -0{\cdot}25\)

\(\mathrm{I} = \left(-0{\cdot}25\right)\times\left(1{\cdot}8\right)\ \Rightarrow\ \mathrm{I} = -0{\cdot}45\ \mathrm{m}\)

Marks: 1 for the ray diagram, 2 for obtaining the relation, 1 for the position of the image, 1 for its height.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the question asks for \(v\) in terms of \(u\) and \(\mathrm{R}\), so it is worth taking the scheme's last line one step further. Using \(f = \mathrm{R}/2\),

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{2}{\mathrm{R}} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{2u - \mathrm{R}}{u\mathrm{R}}\ \Rightarrow\ v = \dfrac{u\mathrm{R}}{2u - \mathrm{R}}\)

In part (ii), the positive \(v\) means the image forms on the side of the lens AWAY from the person, \(1{\cdot}25\ \mathrm{m}\) from it, so the image is real; the negative magnification means it is INVERTED; and its size is \(0{\cdot}45\ \mathrm{m}\), that is \(45\ \mathrm{cm}\) tall. Since the object is well outside the focus of a converging lens, a real, inverted, diminished image is exactly what should be expected before any arithmetic is done — a useful check on the signs.

rows.stem:
(i) Draw a ray diagram showing refraction of a ray of light through a triangular glass prism. Hence, obtain the relation for the refractive index \((\mu)\) in terms of angle of prism (A) and angle of minimum deviation \((\delta_m)\).
(ii) The radii of curvature of the two surfaces of a concave lens are 20 cm each. Find the refractive index of the material of the lens if its power is \(-5{\cdot}0\) D.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) The scheme prints the prism ray diagram: a triangular prism \(\mathrm{ABC}\) with refracting angle \(\mathrm{A}\) at the apex; a ray \(\mathrm{PQ}\) incident at \(\mathrm{Q}\) on face \(\mathrm{AB}\) at an angle of incidence \(i\) and refracted at \(r_1\); the ray travelling to \(\mathrm{R}\) on face \(\mathrm{AC}\), where it makes the angle \(r_2\) with the normal and emerges as \(\mathrm{RS}\) at the angle of emergence \(e\); the produced incident and emergent rays meeting at \(\mathrm{M}\) with the deviation \(\delta\) between them, and \(\mathrm{N}\) the point where the two normals meet.

In the quadrilateral \(\mathrm{AQNR}\), two of the angles — at the vertices \(\mathrm{Q}\) and \(\mathrm{R}\) — are right angles. Therefore the sum of the other angles of the quadrilateral is \(180^\circ\):

\(\angle\mathrm{A} + \angle\mathrm{QNR} = 180^\circ\)

From the triangle \(\mathrm{QNR}\), \(r_1 + r_2 + \angle\mathrm{QNR} = 180^\circ\). Comparing these two equations:

\(r_1 + r_2 = \mathrm{A}\) ..... (i)

The total deviation \(\delta\) is the sum of the deviations at the two faces:

\(\delta = \left(i - r_1\right) + \left(e - r_2\right)\ ,\qquad\text{that is}\qquad \delta = i + e - \mathrm{A}\) ..... (ii)

When \(\delta = \delta_m\), \(i = e\) and \(r_1 = r_2\).

From (i): \(2r = \mathrm{A}\), or \(r = \dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{2}\).

From (ii): \(\delta_m = 2i - \mathrm{A}\), or \(i = \dfrac{\mathrm{A} + \delta_m}{2}\).

\(\mu = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{A} + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{2}}\)

(ii) Given \(\mathrm{P} = -5\ \mathrm{D}\), so

\(f\ \left(\text{in cm}\right) = \dfrac{100}{-5} = -20\ \mathrm{cm}\)

Using the lens maker's formula \(\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\mu - 1\right)\left[\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1} - \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}\right]\):

\(\dfrac{1}{-20} = \left(\mu - 1\right)\left[\dfrac{1}{-20} - \dfrac{1}{+20}\right]\)

\(\dfrac{1}{-20} = \left(\mu - 1\right)\left[-\dfrac{1}{10}\right]\ ;\qquad \mu - 1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(\Rightarrow\ \mu = \dfrac{3}{2} = 1{\cdot}5\)

Marks: 1 for the ray diagram, 2 for obtaining the relation, 2 for the refractive index.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the signs are what make part (ii) work, and they are the easiest thing to lose. For a biconcave lens with light travelling from left to right, the first surface curves towards the incoming light so its centre of curvature lies on the incoming side, giving \(\mathrm{R}_1 = -20\ \mathrm{cm}\); the second surface has its centre on the outgoing side, giving \(\mathrm{R}_2 = +20\ \mathrm{cm}\). Taking both radii positive would make the bracket zero and force \(\mu - 1\) to be infinite, which is the usual symptom of the convention having been skipped.

A note on the printed scheme rather than on the physics: its mark-split box for part (i) calls the prism 'rectangular' where the question and the scheme's own drawing and derivation are all for a TRIANGULAR prism. Only the heading slipped.

On part (i) itself, the physical content of \(i = e\) at minimum deviation is that the path through the prism is symmetric — the ray inside runs parallel to the base — and the deviation-versus-incidence curve is flat there, so a small change of incidence produces almost no change of deviation. That is why \(\delta_m\) can be measured accurately, and it is the basis of the standard laboratory method of finding \(\mu\) for a glass prism.

rows.stem: How long does an electron take to strike the edge ?
rows.context: A beam of electrons moving horizontally with a velocity of \(3 \times 10^{7}\) m/s enters a region between two plates as shown in the figure. A suitable potential difference is applied across the plates such that the electron beam just strikes the edge of the lower plate.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the passage says only ‘as shown in the figure’ and every number the sub-parts need is in the drawing.
