Described: two horizontal parallel plates, each drawn as a pair of lines, with a vertical dimension arrow to the right of them labelled 1 cm for the plate separation and a horizontal dimension arrow beneath them labelled 3 cm for the plate length; an electron is drawn as a dot with a short arrow entering horizontally from the left. Withheld: WHERE between the plates the electron enters, which is what fixes the vertical deflection. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(a) The electron strikes the edge after travelling 3 cm horizontally, along the \(x\)-axis.

\(\mathrm{S}_x = v_x\times t\)

\(3\times 10^{-2} = \left(3\times 10^{7}\right)\times t\)

\(t = 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{s}\)

Marks: ½ for the relation, ½ for the value.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the horizontal motion is unaccelerated. The field between the plates is vertical, so it changes only the vertical velocity; the horizontal component stays at \(3\times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) throughout, and the crossing time follows from the plate LENGTH alone. That \(3\ \mathrm{cm}\) is read off the figure, where it is the horizontal dimension marked beneath the plates — the passage never states it.

The phrase 'just strikes the edge' is doing real work here: it means the electron arrives at the far end of the plates at the very instant it reaches the level of the lower plate. So this same \(10^{-9}\ \mathrm{s}\) is the duration of the vertical motion too, which is what makes the later sub-parts solvable.

rows.stem: What is the shape of the path followed by the electron and why ?
rows.context: A beam of electrons moving horizontally with a velocity of \(3 \times 10^{7}\) m/s enters a region between two plates as shown in the figure. A suitable potential difference is applied across the plates such that the electron beam just strikes the edge of the lower plate.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — same shared drawing as Q34 (a); flagged on every sibling because image_url is per question. Described: two horizontal parallel plates with a 1 cm separation and a 3 cm length marked by dimension arrows, and an electron drawn as a dot with a short arrow entering horizontally from the left. Withheld: where between the plates it enters. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(b) The shape of the path is a parabola.

Reason: the force, and hence the acceleration, is in a fixed direction perpendicular to the initial velocity.

Marks: ½ for the shape, ½ for the reason.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: this is exactly the projectile problem, with the constant electric force taking the place of gravity. Taking the origin at the point of entry, with \(x\) horizontal and \(y\) vertical,

\(x = v_x t\ ,\qquad y = -\dfrac{1}{2}a t^{2}\)

Eliminating \(t\) gives

\(y = -\dfrac{a}{2v_x^{2}}\,x^{2}\)

which is of the form \(y\propto x^{2}\) — a parabola. The essential conditions are that the accelerating force is CONSTANT in both magnitude and direction and that it is not parallel to the initial velocity; if it were parallel the path would be a straight line, and if it changed direction with the velocity, as a magnetic force does, the path would curve into a circle instead.

Once the electron passes beyond the plates the field ends, so from that point it travels in a straight line along the tangent to the parabola.

rows.stem: Find the potential difference applied.
rows.context: A beam of electrons moving horizontally with a velocity of \(3 \times 10^{7}\) m/s enters a region between two plates as shown in the figure. A suitable potential difference is applied across the plates such that the electron beam just strikes the edge of the lower plate.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — same shared drawing as Q34 (a); flagged on every sibling because image_url is per question. The vertical deflection this sub-part needs is stated NOWHERE in the passage and follows only from the drawing. Described: two horizontal parallel plates with a 1 cm separation and a 3 cm length marked by dimension arrows, and an electron drawn as a dot with a short arrow entering horizontally from the left. Withheld: where between the plates it enters. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(c) Along the \(y\)-direction:

\(\mathrm{S}_y = u_y t + \dfrac{1}{2}a_y t^{2}\)

\(-0{\cdot}5\times 10^{-2} = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}a_y\left(10^{-9}\right)^{2}\)

\(a_y = -10^{16}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)

Magnitude of acceleration:

\(a_y = \dfrac{e\mathrm{E}}{m} = \dfrac{e}{m}\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{V}}{l}\right)\)

\(\mathrm{V} = \dfrac{10^{16}\times 9{\cdot}1\times 10^{-31}\times 1\times 10^{-2}}{1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19}}\)

\(\mathrm{V} = 568{\cdot}75\ \mathrm{V}\)

Marks: ½ for the acceleration, ½ for the formula, ½ for the substitution, ½ for the value.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: two numbers in that working come from the FIGURE and not from the passage, and it is worth being explicit about both.

The vertical drop used is \(0{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{cm}\), which is HALF the plate separation, because the drawing shows the beam entering midway between the two plates; 'just strikes the edge of the lower plate' therefore means falling through half the gap. The initial vertical velocity \(u_y\) is zero because the beam enters horizontally, which is why the first term of the kinematic equation drops out.

The other figure-derived number is \(l = 1\ \mathrm{cm} = 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}\), the plate SEPARATION — not the 3 cm length used in part (a). It is the distance across which the potential difference acts, so it is what enters \(\mathrm{E} = \mathrm{V}/l\). Putting the pieces together,

\(\mathrm{V} = \dfrac{a_y\,m\,l}{e} = \dfrac{10^{16}\times 9{\cdot}1\times 10^{-31}\times 10^{-2}}{1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19}} = 568{\cdot}75\ \mathrm{V}\)

and the corresponding field is \(\mathrm{E} = \mathrm{V}/l \approx 5{\cdot}7\times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}\).

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: Find the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field which should be created in the space between the plates so that the electron beam goes straight undeviated.
rows.context: A beam of electrons moving horizontally with a velocity of \(3 \times 10^{7}\) m/s enters a region between two plates as shown in the figure. A suitable potential difference is applied across the plates such that the electron beam just strikes the edge of the lower plate.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — same shared drawing as Q34 (a); flagged on every sibling because image_url is per question. Described: two horizontal parallel plates with a 1 cm separation and a 3 cm length marked by dimension arrows, and an electron drawn as a dot with a short arrow entering horizontally from the left. Withheld: where between the plates it enters, and the sense of the electric field between the plates — this sub-part asks for a DIRECTION. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(c) For the beam to pass through undeviated, the electric and magnetic forces must balance:

\(\left|q\mathrm{E}\right| = \left|qv\mathrm{B}\right|\ ;\qquad \mathrm{B} = \dfrac{\mathrm{E}}{v} = \left(\dfrac{m a_y}{e}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{v}\right)\)

Along the \(y\)-direction:

\(\mathrm{S}_y = u_y t + \dfrac{1}{2}a_y t^{2}\)

\(-0{\cdot}5\times 10^{-2} = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}a_y\left(10^{-9}\right)^{2}\ ;\qquad a_y = -10^{16}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)

\(\mathrm{B} = \left(\dfrac{9{\cdot}1\times 10^{-31}\times 10^{16}}{1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19}}\right)\times\left(\dfrac{1}{3\times 10^{7}}\right)\)

\(\mathrm{B} = 1{\cdot}9\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{T}\)

The direction of the magnetic field will be out of the plane of the paper.

Marks: ½ for the balance condition, ½ for the acceleration, ½ for the magnitude, ½ for the direction.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the bracket \(\dfrac{m a_y}{e}\) is simply the electric field strength written another way, since \(a_y = e\mathrm{E}/m\). Numerically \(\mathrm{E} = \dfrac{9{\cdot}1\times 10^{-31}\times 10^{16}}{1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19}} = 5{\cdot}7\times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}\), which agrees with \(\mathrm{V}/l = 568{\cdot}75/10^{-2}\) obtained in the other branch of this sub-part. The condition \(v = \mathrm{E}/\mathrm{B}\) is the velocity-selector relation used in mass spectrometers and in Thomson's measurement of \(e/m\), and it picks out one speed only — particles faster or slower than \(\mathrm{E}/\mathrm{B}\) are still deflected.

The direction is worth checking rather than quoting. Take \(\hat{i}\) along the beam, to the right; \(\hat{j}\) vertically upwards; and \(\hat{k}\) out of the plane of the paper. The beam is deflected DOWNWARDS towards the lower plate, so the electric force on the electron is along \(-\hat{j}\) and the magnetic force must be along \(+\hat{j}\) to cancel it. For an electron \(\vec{\mathrm{F}} = \left(-e\right)\vec{v}\times\vec{\mathrm{B}}\); putting \(\vec{\mathrm{B}} = \mathrm{B}\hat{k}\),

\(\vec{v}\times\vec{\mathrm{B}} = v\mathrm{B}\left(\hat{i}\times\hat{k}\right) = -v\mathrm{B}\,\hat{j}\ ,\qquad \vec{\mathrm{F}} = \left(-e\right)\left(-v\mathrm{B}\hat{j}\right) = +ev\mathrm{B}\,\hat{j}\)

which is upward, as required. So the field must indeed point out of the plane of the paper.

rows.stem: How will the width of central maximum be affected if the wavelength of light is increased ?
rows.context: Diffraction of light is bending of light around the corners of an object whose size is comparable with the wavelength of light. Diffraction actually defines the limits of ray optics. This limit for optical instruments is set by the wavelength of light. An experimental arrangement is set up to observe the diffraction pattern due to a single slit.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(a) \(\beta_0\propto\lambda\). \(\beta_0\) will increase with an increase in wavelength.

Marks: 1.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the width of the central maximum in single-slit diffraction is

\(\beta_0 = \dfrac{2\lambda\mathrm{D}}{a}\)

where \(a\) is the slit width and \(\mathrm{D}\) the slit-to-screen distance. Both are fixed by the apparatus, so the width is directly proportional to the wavelength: red light gives a noticeably broader central band than blue light through the same slit, and if the two are used together the red edges of the pattern extend further out.

rows.stem: Under what condition is the first minimum obtained ?
rows.context: Diffraction of light is bending of light around the corners of an object whose size is comparable with the wavelength of light. Diffraction actually defines the limits of ray optics. This limit for optical instruments is set by the wavelength of light. An experimental arrangement is set up to observe the diffraction pattern due to a single slit.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(b) When the path difference \(a\theta = \lambda\), or at an angle \(\theta\approx\lambda/a\).

Marks: 1.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the standard argument divides the slit into two halves. Take a point in the upper half and the point exactly \(a/2\) below it; light from the pair differs in path by \(\dfrac{a}{2}\sin\theta\). When the path difference across the WHOLE slit is \(a\sin\theta = \lambda\), every such pair differs by \(\lambda/2\), so the two contributions cancel — and since the halves can be paired off completely, the whole slit gives zero.

For the small angles usual in diffraction, \(\sin\theta\approx\theta\), which is the form the scheme writes. Note that the condition \(a\sin\theta = \lambda\) is a MINIMUM here, whereas in two-slit interference \(d\sin\theta = \lambda\) is a maximum — the same-looking equation means opposite things, because one comes from the cancellation of a continuous distribution and the other from the reinforcement of two discrete sources.

rows.stem: Write two points of difference between interference and diffraction patterns.
rows.context: Diffraction of light is bending of light around the corners of an object whose size is comparable with the wavelength of light. Diffraction actually defines the limits of ray optics. This limit for optical instruments is set by the wavelength of light. An experimental arrangement is set up to observe the diffraction pattern due to a single slit.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme (any two of the following differences):

| Interference pattern | Diffraction pattern |
|---|---|
| All the maxima are equally spaced. | The width of the central bright maximum is twice the width of the other maxima. |
| The dark fringe has zero intensity. | The dark fringe is not completely dark. |
| All the maxima are of the same intensity. | There is a sharp decrease in the intensity of the maxima after the central bright maximum. |
| It is obtained by the superposition of two waves originating from two sources or slits. | It is obtained by the superposition of waves from points on a single slit. |

The scheme also prints the two intensity graphs: for interference, a train of equally spaced peaks of equal height plotted against path difference; for diffraction, one tall central peak flanked by much weaker secondary maxima plotted against the diffraction angle.

Marks: 1 + 1.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: all four rows follow from a single structural difference. Interference superposes a FINITE number of contributions — two, in Young's experiment — so the resultant swings between \(2a\) and \(0\) in amplitude; every maximum is equally strong and every minimum is exactly dark.

Diffraction superposes a CONTINUOUS distribution of contributions from every point across one slit. Away from the centre these cancel only partially, which is why the minima are not perfectly dark and the secondary maxima are far weaker than the central one — the first secondary maximum has only about 4 per cent of the central intensity. The central maximum is twice as wide because it spans from the first minimum on one side to the first minimum on the other, while each later maximum lies between two consecutive minima.

rows.stem: Two students are separated by a 7 m partition wall in a room 10 m high. If both light and sound waves can bend around obstacles, how is it that the students are unable to see each other even though they can converse easily ?
rows.context: Diffraction of light is bending of light around the corners of an object whose size is comparable with the wavelength of light. Diffraction actually defines the limits of ray optics. This limit for optical instruments is set by the wavelength of light. An experimental arrangement is set up to observe the diffraction pattern due to a single slit.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(c) The opening, or slit, is 3 m, which is of the order of the wavelength of sound waves, whereas it is very large compared with the wavelength of light. Hence sound can bend around the obstacle while light cannot.

Marks: 2.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the \(3\ \mathrm{m}\) is the gap ABOVE the partition — the room is \(10\ \mathrm{m}\) high and the wall is \(7\ \mathrm{m}\), so \(10 - 7 = 3\ \mathrm{m}\) is the aperture the waves must diffract through. The quantity that decides how much a wave spreads after an aperture of width \(a\) is the ratio \(\lambda/a\).

Audible sound has wavelengths from a few centimetres up to several metres — a note at \(110\ \mathrm{Hz}\) has \(\lambda\approx 3\ \mathrm{m}\) — so here \(\lambda/a\) is of order 1 and the sound spreads through a wide angle after passing the gap, filling both halves of the room. Visible light has \(\lambda\approx 5\times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}\), so

\(\dfrac{\lambda}{a}\approx\dfrac{5\times 10^{-7}}{3}\approx 2\times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{rad}\)

an utterly negligible spread. Light therefore travels in effectively straight lines past the wall, casting a sharp geometrical shadow, and the students remain out of each other's sight while hearing each other perfectly well.
